title: DampFree 300g Disposable Moisture Absorbers 2 Pack $2.95 + Delivery ($0 Metro OnePass / C&C / in Store) @ Bunnings
body:
Deal: DampFree 300g Disposable Moisture Absorbers 2 Pack $2.95 + Delivery ($0 Metro OnePass / C&C / in Store) @ Bunnings

[prelude] Damn those reviews are pretty bad. I swear these used to be good, but maybe they've been enshittified
[mrhugo] The people who leave those reviews are f'ed in the head. Calcium chloride is calcium chloride. It's a desiccant, not a mains powered dehumidifier.
They think just because they leave them next to a window they will mechanically remove mosture from the window and fill up in the morning. It's works on hygroscopic attraction, its a slow burn it takes months (like 6m) to fill. Stick it behind your shoes in a cupboard, or in the pantry those places.
Use cases people, Calcium chloride, silica, dehumidifier. I use them all, different use cases.
Dropping the relative humidity (RH) in a room/house = dehumidifier, think 750W 10L per day.
Keeping a moisture out of a mostly closed space = calcium chloride desiccant (this)
Keeping items with strict RH levels managed, e.g cameras, shoes (avoiding hydrolysis) = sealed bag or box with orange silica (rechargeable) but must be sealed, or it will fill in hours.
[elitistphoenix] Can someone recommend a good rechargeable one?
[yippy] I've got some Wisedry 500g pouches form Amazon.
[mrhugo] Be careful with 500g bags. You can pull the relative humidity way too low.
I buy the big 6kg loose beads and just measure up 50g or 100g mesh bags. It's easy to see them change colour as they saturate. Just monitor RH% for your application. Silica isn't an easy thing to manage. If you think you're going to low before you reach equilibrium then it's best to remove the silica.
For example my cameras and lens I like to keep around 50% RH, so once I get sub 50 I remove the silica. I started off with 200g and after a few days I was getting 40% which isn't good for oil seperation in the lens.
If the box or storage isn't sealed you will just pull moisture out of the air which will saturate in hours.
To recharge them, get a baking tray from Kmart and follow the temperature directions and duration, and don't overload.
[yippy] I use them in airtight tubs to store my 3d printer filament, they work fine for my use case. It keeps the humidity at about 15%. I've got 10 year old pla filament that still prints fine.
[prelude] I used to use them in cupboards (Queenslander with mould problems) and just refill them from a bulk pack of desiccant. Replacing the entire thing would be pretty wasteful
[topherboi] What would you recommend as an eco-friendly alternative?
[justtoreply] If you can put a mains powered unit, do that. It's proven cheaper in the long run. If you can't fit such a unit then there are versions of desiccant that can be microwaved and reused.
[RichardF89] damn just received it today, and then the price dropped.
[RexyG] I had one each for the two bathrooms and it takes a while to notice the results. Initially, I thought these were useless… but after about a month or two, I noticed water inside the translucent container.
[baaatender] It definitely reduces mould and musky smell in my wardrobes. There is significantly less micro water beads clinging to walls and clothes.
[mrvaluepack] why bathroom? what a waste of money. you need to put it in an enclosed area or you might as well leave it outside.
[RexyG] Bathrooms are literally one of the best places to use it… I always open the window but this helps as a bonus to control and prevent mould, mildew and odors. Clearly works and for the price it's far from a waste!
[Jack D Price] I put two in my car, keeps the car smelling fresh, and never musky
[buku] Not quite as cheap as this initially but kmart sells moisture absorbers, containers, and refills which would work out cheaper in the long run. https://www.kmart.com.au/search/?searchTerm=Moisture%20Absor…
[hen dawg] Maybe give this a try to really do it for cheap https://youtu.be/KuFnPBlbzuk?si=7ThTMt28Oh-fwUqR
[MrKnowItAll] Interesting, these seem to use calcium chloride crystals which are significantly better at absorbing moisture than silica gel and regenerating them seems to be a similar process as with silica gel as well. Gonna pick up a few to put in various cupboards at home that hold all my filament.. all 170 rolls :D Cheers OP!
[MrKnowItAll] Not bait haha just someone looking to save a few bucks on silica gel and time on drying filament for half a day.
My current cheap-ass method is opening the gel that comes with the filament rolls and storing it to eventually pour into larger printed containers - but it's super slow going lol
[Daabido] Nah. He’s not getting engaged with that setup.
[dufflover] regenerating them seems to be a similar process as with silica gel as well.
That's not what Dr. Google is telling me. Carefully dehydrating at 200+ degrees in the right container vs simply just throwing in the silica gel packs and stuff into my filament dryer (food dehydrator lol) at 60-65 for a few hours.
I actually use a combination. The individual rolls have the silica gel beads but the cupboard and totes have this type in there.
[jeimuzu] These work pretty well. Still have2x from the previous deal. Time to stock up
